title: Chemical Bonding
prerequisites: Electronic configuration and valency concepts from Chapter 4.
Understanding of ions, cations and anions from Chapter 3.

topics.title: Lewis Symbols and Why Atoms Combine
topics.quick_summary: Atoms combine with each other to attain a stable, noble-gas-like electronic configuration, usually with 8 electrons in the outermost shell (the octet rule), represented visually using Lewis (electron-dot) symbols.

detailed.definition: A Lewis symbol (electron-dot symbol) represents an atom's chemical symbol surrounded by dots equal to the number of electrons in its outermost (valence) shell; the octet rule states that atoms react in such a way that each atom gets eight electrons in its outermost shell, achieving a stable, noble-gas-like electronic configuration.
detailed.key_idea: Only valence (outermost shell) electrons are involved in bond formation — inner shell electrons are not shown in Lewis symbols and play no direct role in chemical bonding.
detailed.working_principle: To achieve a stable octet, an atom can lose electrons (forming a positive ion), gain electrons (forming a negative ion), or share electrons with another atom — these three routes correspond to metallic behaviour, non-metallic behaviour, and covalent bond formation respectively.
applications: Lewis symbols and the octet rule are used to predict how any two elements are likely to bond, and to correctly draw the structure of simple molecules.
Explains why noble gases are chemically inert while alkali metals and halogens are highly reactive (needing to lose or gain just one electron respectively).

topics.real_life: Noble gases like neon and argon almost never react with other elements because their outermost shell is already completely filled — precisely the stable state that all other atoms 'aim for' when they form bonds.
points: Only valence shell electrons are shown as dots in a Lewis symbol; a maximum of 8 dots (4 pairs) surround the symbol.
Octet rule: atoms are most stable with 8 electrons in the outermost shell (2 for the very first, K, shell — the duplet rule for elements like hydrogen and helium).
Three ways to satisfy the octet: lose electrons, gain electrons, or share electrons with another atom.
Elements with a nearly-full or nearly-empty valence shell (like halogens or alkali metals) are generally the most reactive.
mistakes: Including inner-shell electrons while drawing a Lewis symbol — only valence electrons are ever shown.
Forgetting that hydrogen and helium follow the duplet rule (stable with just 2 electrons), not the octet rule, since their only shell (K) holds a maximum of 2.
topics.memory_hook: 'Only the OUTER electrons show up as dots — that's the octet's secret plot.'
topics.advanced: The octet rule, while an excellent general guide for main-group elements, has known exceptions (like boron trifluoride with only 6 electrons around boron, or sulphur hexafluoride with 12 electrons around sulphur) — these exceptions are explored more deeply in advanced organic and inorganic chemistry.

topics.title: Ionic Bonding
topics.quick_summary: An ionic bond forms through the complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom, creating oppositely charged ions that attract each other electrostatically.

detailed.definition: An ionic (electrovalent) bond is the electrostatic force of attraction that holds together oppositely charged ions, formed when one atom (usually a metal) completely transfers one or more electrons to another atom (usually a non-metal).
detailed.key_idea: Ionic bonding is favoured between elements with a large difference in their tendency to lose or gain electrons — typically a metal with 1, 2, or 3 valence electrons (which loses them easily) combined with a non- metal with 5, 6, or 7 valence electrons (which gains electrons easily).
detailed.working_principle: The metal atom loses electron(s) to attain a stable configuration, becoming a positively charged cation; the non-metal atom gains those same electron(s) to attain its own stable configuration, becoming a negatively charged anion; the resulting oppositely charged ions are held together by a strong electrostatic force, arranged in a repeating 3D pattern called a crystal lattice.
applications: Explains the properties of common ionic compounds like salt (NaCl) and household bases like sodium hydroxide.
Ionic compounds' high melting points, hardness, and conductivity in molten/dissolved states (but not in solid state) are all consequences of this bonding pattern.

topics.real_life: Common salt (sodium chloride) forms when a sodium atom transfers its single outer electron to a chlorine atom, creating Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are held together by strong electrostatic attraction in a crystal lattice.
points: Ionic bonds typically form between metals (electron donors) and non-metals (electron acceptors).
Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points due to the strong electrostatic forces holding the crystal lattice together.
Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water (since ions become free to move) but not in the solid state (ions are fixed in the lattice).
Ionic compounds are generally soluble in polar solvents like water and insoluble in non-polar solvents.
mistakes: Believing solid ionic compounds conduct electricity — they do NOT conduct in the solid state because the ions are rigidly fixed in place; conduction only happens once ions are free to move (molten or dissolved).
Assuming ionic bonds form between any two different elements — they specifically require a large difference in electron-losing/gaining tendency, typically a metal paired with a non-metal.
topics.memory_hook: 'Metal LOSES, Non-metal GAINS — opposite charges, strongly it remains.'
topics.advanced: The overall strength of an ionic bond (called lattice energy) increases with higher ionic charge and smaller ionic size — this single trend explains why magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride (Na⁺ and Cl⁻).

topics.title: Covalent Bonding & Polarity
topics.quick_summary: A covalent bond forms when two atoms mutually share one or more pairs of electrons to complete their octets, and the resulting bond can be non-polar or polar depending on the electronegativity difference between the atoms.

detailed.definition: A covalent bond is a chemical bond formed by the mutual sharing of one or more pairs of electrons between two atoms, with each shared pair counting towards the octet of both atoms involved. A non-polar covalent bond forms between identical atoms (equal sharing, no charge separation); a polar covalent bond forms between different atoms with unequal electron-attracting ability, creating a partial positive and partial negative end (a dipole).
detailed.key_idea: Covalent bonding occurs between two non-metal atoms, both of which need to gain electrons to complete their octet — since neither can afford to fully give up electrons, they instead share them.
detailed.working_principle: Depending on how many electron pairs are shared, a covalent bond is classified as single (1 pair, e.g., H–H), double (2 pairs, e.g., O=O), or triple (3 pairs, e.g., N≡N); the greater the number of shared pairs, the shorter and stronger the bond. Polarity arises from a difference in electronegativity (the tendency of an atom to attract shared electrons) — the more electronegative atom pulls the shared pair closer, gaining a partial negative charge (δ⁻), leaving the other atom with a partial positive charge (δ⁺).
applications: Covalent bonding explains the structure and properties of the vast majority of organic and everyday molecules, including water, carbon dioxide, methane, and all biomolecules.
Bond polarity explains why water is an excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances (like sugar and salt) but does not mix with non-polar substances (like oil).

topics.real_life: The oxygen molecule (O₂) we breathe is held together by a covalent bond where both oxygen atoms equally share electron pairs, while the water molecule (H₂O) has polar covalent bonds because oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does.
points: Covalent bonds form between two non-metals, sharing electron pairs (not transferring them).
Single bond = 1 shared pair; double bond = 2 shared pairs; triple bond = 3 shared pairs — bond strength and bond order increase, while bond length decreases, from single to triple.
Covalent compounds generally have lower melting/boiling points than ionic compounds and are usually poor conductors of electricity.

Non-polar covalent bond: atoms of the same or very similar electronegativity (e.g., H₂, Cl₂, O₂); polar covalent bond: atoms of noticeably different electronegativity (e.g., H–O in water, H–Cl in hydrochloric acid).
mistakes: Assuming all covalent bonds are non-polar — bonds between different non-metal elements (like C–O or H–Cl) are typically polar due to differing electronegativities.
Confusing bond polarity (a property of one individual bond) with the overall polarity of the whole molecule (which also depends on the molecule's 3D shape and symmetry).
topics.memory_hook: 'Same wants become Even (non-polar); Different wants make one end Negative & one Positive (polar).'
topics.advanced: Dipole moment is the quantitative measure of a bond's or molecule's overall polarity, defined as the product of the magnitude of charge and the distance between the charge centres — it is why carbon dioxide (linear, symmetrical, polar bonds cancel out) is overall non-polar despite having two polar C=O bonds, while water (bent shape) is overall polar.
